newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Quiet polling day in Indonesia's former capital.
newsitem.headline: Quiet polling day in Indonesia's former capital.

text.p: The sultan of Yogyakarta led hundreds of thousands of people in voting in the ancient city and former capital of Indonesia on Thursday.
Polling was peaceful, despite days of anti-government protests during the four-week campaign, witnesses said.

Clad in a grey suit and accompanied by his wife Queen Hemas, Sri Sultan Hamengkubuwono X -- one of the country's highest profile royal figures -- cast his ballot at a polling station next to the grand palace.
Elsewhere, residents of the city visited hundreds of polling booths located in its small alleys and by-lanes.
The city centre was quiet and many shops were closed, as most of Yogyakarta's two million eligible voters had gone to exercise their vote, witnesses said.
Yogyakarta is also home to several universities and is known for a tradition of student protests.
During the campaign, supporters of the Moslem-based United Development Party (PPP) staged numerous protests against the ruling Golkar party after an attack on the PPP headquarters in the city.
In some protests, PPP supporters carried mock coffins and burned incense that they said symbolised the death of democracy. There were also demonstrations by students who said they would not vote.

Hamengkubowono, who is a candidate for Golkar in the House of Representatives and has a reputation for fairness, said he did not blame the students for the protests, but added that he hoped they would use their right to vote.

"We know that things have changed. I think (protests) are the form to express aspirations. I just hope that people in Yogyakarta will use their rights to vote," Hamengkubuwono told Reuters after casting his ballot.
"I personally believe, despite all the things that have happened, this year's election in Yogyakarta is better than the election in 1992," he added.
Hamengkubuwono's wife is a Golkar candidate for the local legislative body.
Yogyakarta once was Indonesia's capital when the Dutch tried to regain control in the country after World War Two.

The PPP, Golkar and the other minority party, the Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party are contesting elections for 425 seats in the House of Representatives. The other 75 seats are allocated for the military, which does not vote.

Golkar, which has been in power for most of President Suharto's 30-year tenure, is seeking to push its share of the vote to over 70 percent in this year's election from 68 percent at the last polls in 1992.
